web_evidence.title: The Big Read: The Grapes of Wrath — Lesson Three, Narrative and Point of View
web_evidence.note: The National Endowment for the Arts guide explicitly identifies the novel’s narrator as a limited-omniscient third-person voice and explains that the narration alternates in focus between the Joads and migrants collectively.

web_evidence.title: Narration — Prose Fiction: An Introduction
web_evidence.note: An academic narratology textbook gives The Grapes of Wrath as an example of third-person fiction told by a narrator who does not participate in the story.

web_evidence.title: The Grapes of Wrath as a Multigenre, Multivocal Text
web_evidence.note: The Steinbeck Institute describes the interchapters as heteroglossic mixtures of narrator, authorial, folk, professional, and dialogic voices. This supports treating local first-person social voices as embedded discourse rather than automatically as a new base narrator.

web_evidence.title: Place in John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath and The Red Pony
web_evidence.note: This University of Turku thesis calls Chapter 7 first-person and Chapter 25 third-person, but also explains the contrast as changing focalization through figures such as the car salesman. It is relevant contrary terminology, though it does not establish a continuing first-person narrator alongside the external narrator.

person_note: The diagnostic Goodreads passages repeatedly show a nonparticipating, externally positioned narrator with broad access to individual and collective mental states. First-person material in the sample is overwhelmingly character dialogue, quoted collective formulas, rhetorical identification, or Steinbeck’s paratextual working journal. The novel’s interchapters do vary voice and genre: most notably, Chapter 7 sustains a used-car-salesman monologue, and one scholarly source calls that a first-person change. The Steinbeck Institute’s account of heteroglossia and the chapter’s dramatized salesman focalization make that local social voice better treated as embedded discourse than as an autonomous controlling narrator. Both the NEA guide and an academic narratology textbook explicitly classify the whole novel’s narrator as third-person and nonparticipating. The main residual uncertainty is terminological treatment of Chapter 7, but the controlling base narration remains THIRD.
